output.headline: MI5's Iran operation leads to more than 50 arrests this year
output.bodyHtml:
MI5's counter-Iran operation has led to more than 50 arrests in the UK in the past year, Ken McCallum said, as the agency works to meet what he described as a more aggressive Iran, which he said had threatened other military bases in the UK and was behind the incident at RAF Fairford late last month.

MI5 would create a new unit, McCallum added, to bring together expertise from across government and separate the reality of AI-related risks from the bluster, as part of a wide-ranging annual security update.

The new AI Threat Assessment Centre would help advise both government and the wider public, McCallum said, after highlighting the potential use of AI by hostile states and terrorists, including to possibly develop a novel bioweapon.

A year ago, a 16-year-old from Inverclyde was handed a 10-year prison sentence after he pleaded guilty to planning mass murder by firebombing a Muslim centre in Greenock, McCallum noted.

Extremists with anti-migrant opinions are, however, becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK, the MI5 chief also warned.

McCallum said a shift from radicalised rightwing sentiment to violence was "the most marked trend" in the spy agency's caseload over the past year, contributing to a rise in the overall UK terror threat level.

On the evolving extreme rightwing threat, McCallum said there had been an increase in cases where "extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent", such as planning attacks on migrants and Muslims.

A number of aggressive anti-migrant protests have been held this autumn by the far-right Patriot Platform at Portsmouth and Dover, while racially and religiously motivated offences are running at record levels.

Related: From black-clad agitators to an appeal for 'Tommo's Mum': an unsettling week with the Patriot Platform

McCallum said young people were particularly likely to gravitate towards extreme rightwing terrorism, and at one point this year the Security Service was "investigating a radicalised ... 13-year-old in the UK".

There was a "concerning trend of violence targeted at political figures, religious or community groups", McCallum said, as demonstrated by the killing of the former minister and Reform UK spokesperson, Ann Widdecombe.

On Thursday, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is due to meet his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon for a discussion where the issue of base security in the UK is almost certain to be raised. A week after the Fairford incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from the RAF base, which had been used to attack Iran in the spring and early summer.

Iran, McCallum said, was trying to expand hostile activities in the UK and now had "ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites", including the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire.

Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found.

There was also a hint that Iran had sought to target other bases. "Fairford is not unique in the UK," McCallum said, though he would not be drawn specifically on what other sites had been threatened, or the nature of the threat.

However, allies said his comments were not a reference to RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, where two Latvians were found by police at 2am inside the perimeter of a base used for US and Nato intelligence operations in Europe. They too were subsequently released on police bail.

Iran, though, still has a relatively low level of capability to match its ambitions. Tehran typically hires criminal proxies to carry out operations abroad, so any ability to target a military base "is really a function of the sophistication level of those criminals".

Much of Tehran's increased aggression has been aimed at "British Jewish communities", McCallum said, including terrorist plots and arson attacks against synagogues, businesses and ambulances.

In an unexpected observation, McCallum said he was "particularly focused" on the risk of hostile states or terrorists using AI to generate new, deadly bioweapons, particularly if guardrails introduced by software companies failed.

Last month, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, warned that there were "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development" - and said misuse could have serious consequences.

Liam Booth-Smith, head of Europe policy at Anthropic and a former chief of staff to Rishi Sunak, told the Commons business committee on Tuesday that there was a risk of real harm from the fast-developing technology.

"Without appropriate mitigations, it's possible that real harm could be caused in the space of helping people to create biological or chemical weapons," Booth-Smith said.

The MI5 chief added that AI could also be exploited by cyber hackers, to help terrorists refine their attack plans and even try to use "AI-enabled drones", he said, and to easily produce "propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual".

Russia, the MI5 chief emphasised, remains "aggressor number one" as the Kremlin continues to lash out against the west with assassination plots, explosive threats and cyber-attacks that at times stop "not much short" of conventional warfare.

Moscow tried to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media, and via troll social media accounts, but there was a big difference between "what may have been attempted and what actually resulted", McCallum said.

The UK's relationship with China was "multifaceted", with MI5 focused on Beijing's efforts to steal university research and intellectual property, and obtain political secrets about areas it was interested in.

Overall, threats from hostile states had quadrupled in the last decade and now were running on par with MI5's counter-terrorism mission. "We have again entered a new era of national security," he said.
output.standfirst: MI5 says the operation against Iran has led to more than 50 arrests this year, and it is also planning a new unit to assess AI-related risks, as its chief points to a shift from anti-immigration and anti-Muslim sentiment to violence, and separately to a 'concerning trend' of violence against political and religious figures, including the killing of Ann Widdecombe.
output.progress: A new unit will bring together expertise from across government to separate real AI threats from bluster.

output.headline: Pope Leo's lung operation was 'successful, on schedule and as planned'
output.bodyHtml:
Leo's operation to remove a growth from his lung concluded "successfully, on schedule and as planned", the Vatican said, after tests taken during the surgery confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma.

Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican confirmed late on Tuesday, in a medical bulletin that followed the earlier, more positive statement on how the operation itself had gone.

The Vatican said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was then confirmed during surgery. Leo was in the operating theatre for about three hours, with the operation itself lasting approximately 90 minutes.

In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, Leo said during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup, adding that it was "well-contained" and detected early.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it," he said to the crowds gathered in St Peter's Square.

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said he had seen Leo on Monday night. "We spoke with great serenity," Parolin told Rai News. "He is truly a great example. The announcement came like a bolt out of the blue, nobody expected it. Thank God it was detected immediately, so the operation could take place immediately. Normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved."

The Vatican said that Leo had "now returned to his room" following the operation. Leo, 71, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, is being treated in Rome's Gemelli hospital, where a large crowd greeted his arrival earlier on Tuesday.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio, a practicing Catholic who has met with the pope, said he and his wife were "united in prayers" for Leo following the diagnosis. Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese also wished him a quick recovery, saying he was "a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world."

All of Leo's appointments have been cancelled until 20 October.

Leo is staying in the 10th-floor private-patient wing but not in the papal suite, which is being renovated.

The Chicago-born pope, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, is generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.

Leo travelled to France on a papal visit in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.

The weekly papal audience on Wednesday will be led by Luis Antonio Tagle, a cardinal from the Philippines who last week was elected dean of the college of cardinals - the authority that presides over papal conclaves.

The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish the high-security papal suite.

Leo's predecessor, Francis, spent more than five weeks in the hospital, being treated for bronchitis, which developed into bilateral pneumonia. He died at home in Casa Santa Marta in Vatican City on 21 April 2025, just under a month after being discharged.
output.standfirst: The Vatican says the pontiff's surgery to remove a growth, which was detected early during a checkup, was carried out exactly as planned; tests taken during the operation confirmed a diagnosis of lung cancer.
output.progress: Doctors say the operation went exactly as planned, and the pope has already returned to his room.

output.headline: Anthropic's safety researchers race to get ahead of self-replicating AI
output.bodyHtml:
Anthropic's "frontier red team", the unit tasked with stress-testing AI systems, has published a report exploring whether its models could become "self-replicating" and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners. The idea of the team is to explore the capabilities of their AI models.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the researchers wrote.

In the scenario the team tested, researchers prompted an agent to try to hack internet-connected devices. They found that AI self-replication would only likely work with smaller models, and that homes and small businesses would probably be the first target for such attacks.

The company said these "AI worms", a kind of autonomous malware, could be "months away" from gaining such capabilities. Once out-of-control AI systems reach the capability to hack smart devices, they could spread through networks while dodging detection. In a worst-case scenario, Anthropic said, various AI worms could "swarm" together to attack computer hardware.

Once this happens, the company said, the models could power themselves within these devices without the need of datacenters. Such self-replication would represent a major loss of control of a runaway AI model.

"A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down," the researchers wrote, "since there's no centralized point to shut off."

The devices Anthropic lists as susceptible all come with small built-in AI chips, including smart ovens, smart TVs, automatic lawnmowers, security cameras and video-conferencing units.

The researchers concluded it's unclear what form the AI replication could take. They said it could be a slow model like "digital slime mold", a model that scams people for compute credits or a "powerful cyber model" that rapidly hacks large facilities such as datacenters.

Regardless, the Anthropic researchers said, they're expecting a future "awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control".

Anthropic's new report comes as AI safety concerns have reached a fever pitch. Over the past few months, a steady stream of reports have come from AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, saying their agents are capable of acting on their own and hacking into other companies and government entities.

The revelations have caused researchers, lawmakers and executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, to call for a slowdown and increased guardrails on the burgeoning industry. Despite that, both companies have continued apace to develop and release new models.
output.standfirst: Anthropic's in-house 'frontier red team' is testing whether its AI models could become self-replicating. Such 'AI worms' would be difficult to shut down, and in a worst case could 'swarm' together to attack hardware - a risk the company says could be only months away - and the researchers say systems should be hardened before that happens.
output.progress: Anthropic's red team is testing the risk in advance and pushing to harden systems before self-replication becomes possible.

output.headline: BBC presses ahead with bid to put Trump under oath in $10bn case
output.bodyHtml:
The BBC is asking a federal judge in Florida to compel Donald Trump to confirm and sit for a deposition as part of the president's $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.

"Plaintiff chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation," the BBC's motion reads. "The BBC therefore asks the Court to compel Plaintiff to confirm a date for his deposition, notify the BBC of a secure location where such deposition is possible and any other logistics required to ensure Plaintiff's safety, and sit for the deposition, as the core rules of discovery require."

Magistrate judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett has scheduled a discovery hearing that is likely to touch on the deposition issue for 22 October.

According to a Tuesday filing, the BBC and Trump's legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday. The BBC's lawyers wrote to the judge that they have spent months trying to secure a location for the deposition from Trump's team.

On 28 September, Trump's lawyers told the BBC's counsel that the president "is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance".

While Trump's lawyers said they would follow up quickly with a replacement date, they did not, ultimately suggesting that he would be available in the second or third week of January, well after the deadline to complete the discovery portion of the case. Lawyers for the BBC had pledged to keep the location of the deposition confidential.

As such, the BBC's lawyers are now asking the judge to require Trump's team to schedule the deposition.

"Nearly eight months into discovery, after seven depositions of BBC witnesses, and with only two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself," lawyers for the BBC wrote in the Tuesday motion.

Trump, who has a long history of legal action against media companies, filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025, accusing the network of violating Florida's Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act over the edit of a Panorama documentary that edited together comments he made during a rally on 6 January 2021. The BBC has apologized for the error.

"The formerly respected and now disgraced BBC defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election," a spokesperson for Trump's legal team said in a statement. "The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda. President Trump's powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing."
output.standfirst: The broadcaster has asked a federal judge to compel Donald Trump to confirm a deposition date, after his team cancelled their agreed Friday session citing 'other matters of national importance'.
output.progress: The BBC is asking the court to compel a deposition date, with a discovery hearing already scheduled for 22 October.

output.headline: UK fast-tracks missile deliveries to Ukraine as Burnham welcomes Zelenskyy
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK moves to speed up deliveries of British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect Ukraine from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.

The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: "We are with you for as long as it takes."

In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). The chancellor, John Healey, will separately use meetings at the ongoing International Monetary Fund summit in Bangkok to push other countries to ban Russian LNG.

Announcing the Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing 1.6 billion pound package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat the drone attacks.

These drones are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv.

In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.

"My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.

"It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do. Russia's aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent."

The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth that month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.

Zelenskyy's latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said "was news to him".

Trump is an often wayward ally for Ukraine, and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a "thanks" from Vladimir Putin.

UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. He met Keir Starmer at Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, publicly berated the Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago.

During that trip Zelenskyy was also hosted by King Charles, who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits.
output.standfirst: The UK will speed up deliveries of missiles to help Ukraine counter a new generation of Russian drones, as the prime minister reiterates British backing after the Ukrainian president's latest difficulties with Donald Trump.
output.progress: The UK is speeding up missile deliveries to Ukraine and pushing other countries to ban Russian LNG exports.

output.headline: Court keeps CNN, MS Now and Politico credentialed at the White House
output.bodyHtml:
A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition's lawsuit against the Trump administration plays out.

In his ruling, Judge Timothy Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs "are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims". While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.

"Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House 'hard pass' press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, thereby maintaining the status quo since the Court's entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026," the judge wrote in granting a preliminary injunction requested by the plaintiffs.

During arguments for the preliminary injunction on 8 October, media lawyer Theodore J Boutrous told the judge that Trump had offered a "confession" - in a Time magazine interview the week before - that he was banning the media companies explicitly because of the content of their reporting, not because of any other considerations, such as national security.

"The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump," Boutrous told the judge.

The judge seemed to agree. "President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before," he wrote.

In a statement, Boutrous said of the judge's ruling: "When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers."

The court, he added, "was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this 'unconstitutional ban on the free press' for the foreseeable future".

Kelly had on 24 September granted a 14-day reprieve for the news organizations, which six days earlier had been banned by the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds "as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS".

Related: US justice department investigating TV networks over Trump pool coverage

The organizations filed a lawsuit on 21 September seeking to overturn the ban as a violation of their rights under the US constitution. That temporary restraining order expired on Tuesday, bringing the media companies into court late last week to ask for the preliminary injunction that would lift the ban during the duration of the lawsuit, which could take months.

During arguments at the E Barrett Prettyman Federal Courthouse in Washington, Kelly seemed inclined to lift the ban indefinitely, telling a lawyer for the federal government that his side had "a notice problem" that was "probably the biggest hurdle" they had to overcome.

The Trump White House gave no advance notice to the media companies affected to say that they were at risk of losing their press badges, which the news organizations have said are essential to their ability to cover the administration. While the White House sent letters to the media companies informing them of the ban, they did so post-hoc, after building access had already been cut off, in violation of binding court precedent.

Although the White House has largely adhered to the judge's prior ruling restoring access on a temporary basis, journalists for CNN and Politico have on occasion been prevented from performing "pool duty" - covering the daily activities of the president - because the administration has interpreted the judge's temporary restraining order to solely require access to the White House complex, not smaller spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office.

The judge required the media plaintiffs to post a bond of $1.
output.standfirst: District judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to keep allowing the outlets' journalists in while their lawsuit proceeds, finding they are likely to succeed on their due process and First Amendment claims against the September ban.
output.progress: The judge found the outlets likely to succeed on both their due process and First Amendment claims.

output.headline: Iranian student sentenced to death over a social media post
output.bodyHtml:
In an audio recording released from prison last month, the Iranian student Najmeh Amini appealed for international intervention, calling on the UN, lawyers and rights groups to investigate her case.

"I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice," she said.

"I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams," Amini said. "I have parents who are waiting for me. A family that every night, with the fear of losing me, turns their night into morning."

Human rights groups have raised the alarm after reports that Amini, 23, has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social-media post. Her death sentence is not final and remains subject to appeal before Iran's supreme court.

Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.

A source close to Amini's family told the US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRAI) that Amini was sentenced to death on charges of "sab ol-nabi" (insulting the prophet).

In the second case, Amini was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the regime.

Amini was arrested by security forces during January's nationwide protests, which were suppressed with a deadly crackdown. Thousands were reported killed, while the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested.

Rights groups warn that the Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to instil fear and suppress dissent. According to the Oslo-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), more than 600 executions have already been carried out this year.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of IHRNGO, said Amini's case should be seen as a serious warning.

"Sentencing a young woman to death for what she posted on social media risks normalising the use of the death penalty against peaceful expression and pushing the boundaries of the death penalty even further," he said.

Amiry-Moghaddam added that the Iranian authorities were testing the international community's "tolerance" towards capital punishment. "If the international community does not respond firmly now, cases like this could become far more common," he said.

Under article 262 of Iran's Islamic penal code, insulting the prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. However, article 263 provides exemptions for statements made while intoxicated or without deliberate intent, although offenders may still face up to 74 lashes in certain circumstances.

According to the Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, Amini told the court she had posted the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends, and her defence argued it was a "slip of the tongue".

The presiding judge rejected her defence, reportedly asking: "Why, in that same hallucinatory state, did you not insult other individuals or opponents of the regime, such as America and Israel?"

Related: Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for help

The student's sentencing comes at a time when Iranian lawmakers are seeking to criminalise contact with all foreign media, including posts on social media deemed to be financed by another country.

Elnaz*, 24, who took part in the protests in Tehran in January and was arrested over social-media posts at the height of the war in March, said she lived in constant fear of surveillance.

"I was arrested even though my social-media account was private. So it's not just the regime's cyber-police we have to worry about. There's also this constant mistrust, this feeling that someone is watching me all the time, even when I'm alone in my room.

"I'm scared to post anything on social media ... but after everything they've put us through, do we really have anything left to lose? They can kill us even if we don't post anything on social media."

Although executions in Iran have surged in recent years, reaching their highest level in three decades, death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively rare. The last documented case was on 8 May 2023, when Yousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executed after being convicted of blasphemy-related offences tied to social-media activity.

* Name has been changed to protect her identity
output.standfirst: Najmeh Amini, 23, has appealed for international help, saying: 'I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice.' Rights groups say Tehran is increasingly using capital punishment to suppress dissent, with more than 600 executions already this year.

output.headline: Rules, London's oldest restaurant, is given to the National Trust to secure its future
output.bodyHtml:
When Thomas Rule served his first oyster to diners on Maiden Lane in London's Covent Garden, "mad" George III was on the throne of England, John Adams was US president and William Pitt the Younger had just come up with a wheeze called income tax to pay for the Napoleonic wars.

More than two centuries later, Rules, the restaurant Thomas founded in what became the capital's theatreland, has outlasted nine British monarchs and 45 prime ministers - but has changed hands only three times. The interior of its four-storey home, stuffed with historic playbills and vintage caricatures and gilded antlers, is little changed from the 19th century, nor has the tone of its determinedly meaty menu - think rabbit rillettes, shin of veal and roast guinea fowl.

Rules was beloved by Dickens and Thackeray, inspired Graham Greene and was a favourite of Charlie Chaplin, Laurence Olivier and Ava Gardner. Now the man who bought Rules in 1984 has taken what may be the most significant step in its long history, donating the restaurant's historic home to the National Trust, assured that the heritage charity will "protect this place in a way that no one else could".

"With many years of hard work, and some extraordinary strokes of luck, Rules has survived everything from redevelopment plans and changing tastes to the blitz," JP Mayhew said. By taking on the historic and listed 34-35 Maiden Lane, he added, the National Trust would "[safeguard] its bricks and mortar, its famous interior and its invisible atmosphere too. I am grateful to them for believing in this idea and for protecting this building and two centuries worth of stories for people to enjoy forever".

The 11 million pound "landmark" gift is one of the most valuable in the National Trust's recent history, and will mark its first entry into the restaurant business - although its portfolio includes 39 historic pubs and a number of country house hotels, including Cliveden in Buckinghamshire.

Not that the heritage charity will be taking on the napkin-folding and the slow cooking of pork cheeks. While Mayhew is donating the historic building and its contents, he sold the restaurant business to Ricky McMenemy, its longstanding general manager, in 2022; McMenemy will become a commercial tenant of the National Trust.

"Our involvement, day to day, will probably be very light touch," said Lucy Porten, a national curator for the charity. "It will always be run as a restaurant. We will look after [the building and its contents], but we recognise that they will have to evolve if they are going to continue to meet diners' needs."

Diners, however, can expect little change to the menu, she said - and crucially, no scones. "It's not a National Trust menu, this is a very successful business in its own right. There will be no scones. That's not their business." Nor will there be preferential access or prices for National Trust members, "because it is a business, and it has to be successful," she added. Instead, the charity is exploring options for virtual visits and other ways people could "feel like they are visiting the space" from afar.

It was several years ago when Mayhew first approached the National Trust about a possible gift. Porten said that while "excited by the offer", they looked carefully at whether it was the right organisation to take on the building.

Porten said: "The nature of the National Trust, and the fact we have this extraordinary ability to take on places inalienably, for ever, means that we have to think about what's right for now, but also to think about looking after them for future generations. That's quite a big thing ... It had to be quite a balanced response and decision."

Part of its value to the trust, she said, lay in helping the charity "tell different histories which are hard for us to tell at our other properties".

"You get a sense of all the delicious food which has been enjoyed here, the fine wines that have been consumed, the good company that's been enjoyed. There's something in the air about the conversations and the celebrations, the flirtations, the deals that have been struck, the heartbreak. All that hangs in the air, in a very magical way, [as] the backdrop to lots of different historical moments and lives.

"It's an extraordinary slice of the social history of London, and to have been here for so long - in this site and doing this business - is a very rare and special thing."
output.standfirst: The historic Covent Garden eatery, which has changed hands only three times in 228 years, has been donated to the heritage charity, which will protect the building 'for ever'.
output.progress: Mayhew says he is grateful the Trust is protecting the building and its stories 'for people to enjoy forever'.

output.headline: Tuning in to how a language sounds is the secret to learning it fast
output.bodyHtml:
If you want to get really good at French, Arabic or Hungarian, don't start with rote learning vocabulary and grammar - focus on how they sound instead, research suggests.

The latest findings challenge stereotypes that Britons are less adept at languages. Prof Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, the lead author and professor of second language education at UCL Institute of Education, said: "I do not think British people are biologically bad at languages. The problem is more likely to be that many people receive too little meaningful exposure, combined with teaching methods that do not necessarily train the auditory skills needed to make the most of that limited exposure."

"If you only hear and use the language for a small number of hours each week, having a good ear may make a much bigger difference. Learners with high auditory precision can make very effective use of relatively sparse input, whereas others may need much more exposure before unfamiliar sounds begin to become established," he said.

A new study of how humans learn modern languages has found that the brains of the most talented linguists hear foreign terms as random noise, not words.

Normally, when people learn a language, they try to understand it through the sounds of their native tongue. The more different the foreign language's sounds and pronunciation are from the native language, the harder the new language will probably be to learn.

But the best linguists master even the trickiest pronunciation much more easily. To find out why, researchers at UCL and Tohoku University, Japan, compared the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight changes in pitch, length and tone, in non-speech sounds. Using functional MRI scans, they measured participants' brain activity as they tried to distinguish between English vowel sounds that do not occur in Japanese.

They found that those with higher auditory precision mastered the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners and relied less on the brain's left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Instead, their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds.

With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds.

In contrast, those with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain's left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native language when processing unfamiliar sounds.

Related: Acai, chipotle and gnocchi - and other words you are probably mispronouncing

The findings also suggest schools should focus on sounds much more than just grammar and vocabulary when teaching modern languages, Saito-van Poeteren added.

"Foreign language education should move beyond an approach based on 'more practice' and towards one that develops learners' ear for language learning in line with their auditory characteristics," he said.

Responding to the findings, Prof Padraic Monaghan, professor of cognition at Lancaster University, said: "Traditional language learning relies on structured practice, but our brains are naturally attuned to acquire languages through exposure. This study confirms how vital listening is to learning, though learners vary in their sound sensitivity at least in the early stages of hearing new language sounds."
output.standfirst: A new study finds the most talented linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds like non-speech noise, a finding researchers say challenges stereotypes that Britons are simply bad at languages.
output.progress: Researchers say schools could teach sound-recognition skills directly, helping learners make better use of limited exposure to a new language.
